\chapter{The Noun, And The Ending That Means Two Things}
\label{ch:hi-sangya}
\hlchaptermodality{99}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can make any A1 noun plural, read the oblique form a noun takes in front of a postposition, and put a demonstrative in front of a noun.}

Read the clause a practice paper prints in a personal account -- do bhaashaaen boltii hai -- and tell a plural -e apart from an oblique one by the postposition behind it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bacce]{\hi{बच्चे} — more than one, and an ending you have seen four times}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-bacche-plural}



\begin{quote}
You can say \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}} for one child. Try to say \emph{children}, and notice the track has taught you a great many words and never how to have two of anything.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बच्चे}}
\textbf{\hi{बच्चे}} (\emph{bacce}) — children.

\textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{बच्चा}} — one child. \textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{बच्चे}} — two children.

\begin{cousinweb}
The ending moved from \textbf{-\hi{आ}} to \textbf{-\hi{ए}}, and you have watched that happen four times already:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural or masculine-plural} \\
\midrule
adjectives & \hi{काला} & \hi{काले} \\
the habitual & \hi{बोलता} & \hi{बोलते} \\
the past copula & \hi{था} & \hi{थे} \\
\textbf{a noun} & \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}} & \textbf{\hi{बच्चे}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Nouns bend the same way adjectives do}, which is not a coincidence: to Hindi they are the same kind of word wearing the same endings. Learning noun plurals is not a new system — it is the one system arriving at a new place.

This applies to \textbf{masculine nouns ending in -\hi{आ}} and to those only. A noun shaped otherwise does something else, and the next lessons take those in turn.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what changes with it}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sentence} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\hi{बच्चा} \hi{लंबा} \hi{है।} & The child is tall. \\
\hi{बच्चे} \hi{लंबे} \hi{हैं।} & The children are tall. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three words moved and the reason is one. The noun went plural, so the adjective followed it and the copula followed the adjective. \textbf{Agreement travels outward} from the noun, and once the noun is right the rest is automatic.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{एक} \hi{बच्चा}\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{बच्चे}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बच्चे} \hi{लंबे} \hi{हैं}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which other words in the sentence had to move, and why
  \item the four places you have met the \textbf{-\hi{आ} / -\hi{ए}} change
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a masculine \textbf{-\hi{आ}} noun do in the plural? (Ends in \textbf{-\hi{ए}}.) Which other words follow it? (The adjective and the copula.) Is this a new system? (No — it is the adjective ending arriving on a noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitābeṁ]{\hi{किताबें} — nothing to change, so something is added}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-kitaben}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{बच्चा}} ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}} and swapped it for \textbf{-\hi{ए}}. \textbf{\hi{किताब}} ends in a consonant. Ask yourself what there is to swap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{किताबें}}
\textbf{\hi{किताबें}} (\emph{kitābeṁ}) — books.

\textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{किताब}} — one book. \textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{किताबें}} — two books.

\begin{cousinweb}
A word with no vowel at the end has nothing to exchange, so Hindi \textbf{adds} a syllable: \textbf{-\hi{एँ}}, the same \textbf{-\hi{ए}} as before with a nasal on it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape of the noun} & \textbf{how it makes a plural} \\
\midrule
ends in -\hi{आ} & swaps the ending for -\hi{ए} \\
ends in a consonant & adds -\hi{एँ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the whole difference, and it follows from the shape rather than from a list to memorise: \textbf{change what is there, or add where nothing is.}

Feminine nouns ending in a consonant, like \textbf{\hi{किताब}}, are much the commonest case, and the nasal is what your ear should catch.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the nasal you already write}]
The mark over the ending is the \textbf{anusvāra}, which you have been writing since \textbf{\hi{हैं}} and \textbf{\hi{मिलेंगे}}. It is doing the same job here that it does there: this is a plural, and the nasal is the sign of it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
\hi{किताब} & \hi{किताबें} \\
\hi{रात} & \hi{रातें} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say both aloud and let the nasal fall on the last syllable rather than swallowing it — that is what a listening paper is asking you to hear.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{एक} \hi{किताब}\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{किताबें}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the plural of \textbf{\hi{रात}}
  \item what a consonant-final noun adds, and why it adds rather than swaps
  \item the plural of \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}}, to hear the two side by side
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a consonant-final noun add? (\textbf{-\hi{एँ}}.) Why does it add instead of swapping? (There is no final vowel to swap.) Which mark carries the plural? (The nasal you already write in \textbf{\hi{हैं}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhāṣāẽ]{\hi{भाषाएँ} — an -\hi{आ} ending that does not behave like the others}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-bhashaen}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{भाषा}} ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, exactly like \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}}. Guess its plural from that, and then read on to find out why the guess is wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{भाषाएँ}}
\textbf{\hi{भाषाएँ}} (\emph{bhāṣāẽ}) — languages.

\textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{भाषाएँ}} — two languages. That phrase is printed in a practice paper, in a personal account: \emph{she speaks two languages}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{भाषा}} is \textbf{feminine}, and that is the whole story. The \textbf{-\hi{आ} $\to$ -\hi{ए}} swap belongs to \textbf{masculine} nouns; a feminine noun \textbf{adds} instead, exactly as \textbf{\hi{किताब}} did.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{gender} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
\hi{बच्चा} & masculine & \hi{बच्चे} \\
\hi{किताब} & feminine & \hi{किताबें} \\
\hi{भाषा} & feminine & \hi{भाषाएँ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the question to ask a noun is \textbf{not} \textquotedblleft{}how does it end\textquotedblright{} on its own. It is \textbf{gender first, ending second} — and the two feminine rows do the same thing despite ending differently.

The \textbf{\hi{ए}} is written as a full letter here rather than as a mark, because \textbf{\hi{भाषा}} ends in a vowel and there is nothing for a mark to sit on. That is the same rule that gave you \textbf{\hi{आऊँगा}} and \textbf{\hi{आओगे}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three shapes, in the order to ask them}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ask this} & \textbf{then this} \\
\midrule
is it masculine? & -\hi{आ} swaps to -\hi{ए} \\
is it feminine? & it adds a nasal ending \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two questions and you have the plural of any A1 noun. The number in front — \textbf{\hi{दो}}, \textbf{\hi{तीन}} — does not change either way; Hindi marks the plural on the noun, not on the numeral.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{भाषाएँ}\textquotedblright{} — two languages
  \item the plurals of \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}}, \textbf{\hi{किताब}} and \textbf{\hi{भाषा}} in a row
  \item which question you ask a noun first
  \item why the \textbf{\hi{ए}} is a full letter in this word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \textbf{\hi{भाषा}} not become \textbf{\hi{भाषे}}? (It is feminine; the swap is for masculine nouns.) What do both feminine nouns do? (Add a nasal ending.) Which question comes first? (Gender.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do ādmī]{\hi{दो} \hi{आदमी} — the plural you cannot see}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-aadmi-unchanged}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{आदमी}} is masculine and ends in \textbf{-\hi{ई}}, not \textbf{-\hi{आ}}. You have a rule for \textbf{-\hi{आ}} and a rule for feminine nouns. Notice this word fits neither.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दो} \hi{आदमी}}
\textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{आदमी}} — one man. \textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{आदमी}} — two men.

The word \textbf{does not change}.

\begin{cousinweb}
A masculine noun that does \textbf{not} end in \textbf{-\hi{आ}} has no plural form at all. It stands still, and the sentence around it does the work:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what tells you} & \textbf{how} \\
\midrule
the numeral & \hi{दो}, \hi{तीन} \\
the verb & \hi{हैं} rather than \hi{है} \\
an adjective & \hi{लंबे} rather than \hi{लंबा} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{आदमी} \hi{लंबे} \hi{हैं।}} — Two men are tall. The noun is the only word in that sentence with nothing to show for it.

This is worth expecting rather than being surprised by, because a reading paper will give you an unchanged noun and ask you to count. \textbf{The number lives in the sentence, not always in the word.}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the whole plural system, now complete}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
\hi{बच्चा} (m, -\hi{आ}) & \hi{बच्चे} \\
\hi{आदमी} (m, other) & \hi{आदमी} \\
\hi{किताब} (f) & \hi{किताबें} \\
\hi{भाषा} (f) & \hi{भाषाएँ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four rows and every A1 noun you will meet is in one of them. Two of the four add a nasal, one swaps a vowel, and one does nothing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{एक} \hi{आदमी}\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{आदमी}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{आदमी} \hi{लंबे} \hi{हैं}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three things in that sentence that tell you it is plural
  \item all four rows of the table
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a masculine noun ending in \textbf{-\hi{ई}} do in the plural? (Nothing.) So what tells you there is more than one? (The numeral, the verb and any adjective.) How many shapes does the whole system have? (Four.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ko]{\hi{को} — the word that was inside \hi{आपको}}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-ko}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{आपको}}. Say it slowly, in two pieces, and you have already said this lesson's word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{को}}
\textbf{\hi{को}} (\emph{ko}) — \textquotedblleft{}to,\textquotedblright{} and the marker a definite or human object wears.

\textbf{\hi{आदमी} \hi{को}} — to the man, and also \emph{the man} when he is the thing acted on.

\begin{cousinweb}
You met it fused. \textbf{\hi{आपको}} is \textbf{\hi{आप} + \hi{को}}, and it was named as such when the oblique pronouns arrived. Here it stands on its own, in front of a noun instead of a pronoun, and it is the third postposition the track now has.

It does two jobs that English keeps apart:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{job} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
a recipient & \hi{आदमी} \hi{को} — \emph{to} the man \\
a definite or human object & \hi{आदमी} \hi{को} — the man, as the thing acted on \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The second is the strange one to an English ear. English marks a direct object by word order and nothing else. Hindi puts \textbf{\hi{को}} on an object when it is a \textbf{person} or a \textbf{particular} thing, and leaves it bare otherwise. Spanish does the same with \textbf{a} before a human object, so the demand is not unique to Hindi — only the marker is.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three postpositions, one habit}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{postposition} & \textbf{what it marks} \\
\midrule
\hi{पर} & at a point \\
\hi{से} & from it, or by way of it \\
\hi{को} & to it, or it as a definite object \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All three trail the noun. All three are one syllable. And all three do something to the noun in front of them, which is what the next lesson is about.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{आदमी} \hi{को}\textquotedblright{} — to the man
  \item \textbf{\hi{आपको}} slowly, in its two pieces
  \item the two jobs \textbf{\hi{को}} does
  \item the three postpositions you now have, and what each marks
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\hi{आपको}} made of? (\textbf{\hi{आप}} plus \textbf{\hi{को}}.) When does a direct object take \textbf{\hi{को}}? (When it is a person, or a particular thing.) Which European language marks a human object the same way? (Spanish, with \textbf{a}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bacce ko]{\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को} — the same ending, and this time it is not a plural}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-bacche-ko}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{\hi{बच्चे}} as \emph{children}. Read \textbf{\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}} and notice it cannot mean \emph{to the children} and \emph{one child} at the same time — so which is it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}}
\textbf{\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}} — \textbf{to the child}. One child.

A noun standing in front of a postposition changes shape, and for a masculine \textbf{-\hi{आ}} noun that shape is \textbf{-\hi{ए}} — the same ending the plural uses.

\begin{cousinweb}
This is \textbf{not a new rule}. It is the one the possessives taught you, arriving on a noun:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{plain} & \textbf{in front of a postposition} \\
\midrule
\hi{मेरा} & \hi{मेरा} & \hi{मेरे} \hi{पास} \\
\hi{उसका} & \hi{उसका} & \hi{उसके} \hi{बाद} \\
\textbf{\hi{बच्चा}} & \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}} & \textbf{\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Hindi calls this shape the \textbf{oblique}. Every \textbf{-\hi{आ}} word in the language wears it — possessives, adjectives, and now nouns — and it is always the same \textbf{-\hi{ए}}.

So the track has taught this bend four times on four kinds of word, and this is the fourth and last kind.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: how to tell the two -\hi{ए} apart}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you see} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
\hi{बच्चे} \hi{हैं} & plural — nothing follows the noun \\
\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को} & singular oblique — a postposition follows \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The postposition is the whole signal.} If one is standing behind the noun, the \textbf{-\hi{ए}} is oblique and the noun may well be singular. If nothing is, the \textbf{-\hi{ए}} is a plural.

A plural \emph{in front of} a postposition takes yet another shape, which is one step past A1 — recognise \textbf{\hi{बच्चों} \hi{को}} on a page and leave it there for now.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}\textquotedblright{} — to the child
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बच्चे} \hi{हैं}\textquotedblright{} — and say how many children that is
  \item what tells you which \textbf{\hi{बच्चे}} you are reading
  \item the possessive pair that bends the same way
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many children is \textbf{\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}}? (One.) What forces the noun into that shape? (The postposition behind it.) Which earlier words wore the same \textbf{-\hi{ए}}? (The possessives, in front of a postposition.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yah kitāb]{\hi{यह} \hi{किताब} — the same word, one step to the left}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-yah-kitab}



\begin{quote}
You have \textbf{\hi{यह}} and \textbf{\hi{वह}} as answers to \emph{which one} — standing alone, meaning \emph{this one} and \emph{that one}. Try putting one in front of a noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{यह} \hi{किताब}}
\textbf{\hi{यह} \hi{किताब}} — this book. \textbf{\hi{वह} \hi{आदमी}} — that man.

Nothing is added and nothing bends. The word you already have is placed in front of a noun, and that is the whole of it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how it stands} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
\hi{यह} & this one \\
\hi{यह} \hi{किताब} & this book \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English does exactly the same thing with the same two words — \emph{this} is a pronoun in \emph{this is mine} and a determiner in \emph{this book} — so there is nothing here to translate differently. The reason it needs saying is that the track taught these words \textbf{only} as standalone answers, and a reading paper uses them in front of nouns far more often.

There is a second reason it matters. Hindi has no article, so \textbf{\hi{यह}} and \textbf{\hi{वह}} are what a writer reaches for when \emph{the} would have been enough in English. A sentence that begins \textbf{\hi{वह} \hi{आदमी}} is often best read as \emph{the man} rather than \emph{that man}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what fills the space before a noun}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{in front of the noun} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
nothing & a book, or the book \\
\hi{एक} & one book, a book \\
\hi{यह} / \hi{वह} & this book, that book \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three choices and the reader picks from context. That is the whole of Hindi definiteness at this level, and it is why the track has spent no time on articles: \textbf{there are none to spend it on.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यह} \hi{किताब}\textquotedblright{} — this book
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वह} \hi{आदमी}\textquotedblright{} — that man, or the man
  \item the same two words standing alone, as answers
  \item the three things that can stand in front of a Hindi noun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What changes when \textbf{\hi{यह}} moves in front of a noun? (Nothing — it is placed there.) Why does Hindi lean on these two words more than English does? (It has no article.) How is \textbf{\hi{वह} \hi{आदमी}} often best read? (\emph{The man}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[saṁjñā kī tālikā]{saṁjñā kī tālikā — the noun, on one page}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-repaso-sangya}



\begin{quote}
Name the first question you ask a noun before making it plural, and say why it comes first.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four plurals}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
\hi{बच्चा} (m, -\hi{आ}) & \hi{बच्चे} \\
\hi{आदमी} (m, other) & \hi{आदमी} \\
\hi{किताब} (f, consonant) & \hi{किताबें} \\
\hi{भाषा} (f, -\hi{आ}) & \hi{भाषाएँ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Gender first, ending second. One row swaps a vowel, two add a nasal, and one does nothing at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending that means two things}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you see} & \textbf{how many} & \textbf{why} \\
\midrule
\hi{बच्चे} \hi{लंबे} \hi{हैं} & more than one & nothing follows the noun \\
\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को} & one & a postposition follows \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The postposition is the signal.} That is the single most useful thing in this chapter, because \textbf{-\hi{ए}} is everywhere and a reader who cannot tell the two apart will miscount every sentence that has one.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the space in front of the noun}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{before the noun} & \textbf{after the noun} \\
\midrule
nothing, \hi{एक}, \hi{यह}, \hi{वह} & \hi{पर}, \hi{से}, \hi{को} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A Hindi noun phrase is a noun with an optional word in front and an optional word behind. Everything this chapter taught fits in that one picture.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four plurals in a row
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बच्चे} \hi{लंबे} \hi{हैं}\textquotedblright{}, and say how many children each has
  \item the three postpositions, and the three things that go in front
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{भाषाएँ}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यह} \hi{किताब}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tells you an \textbf{-\hi{ए}} is oblique rather than plural? (A postposition behind it.) Which two rows add a nasal? (Both feminine ones.) Which noun shape does nothing at all? (A masculine noun not ending in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do bhāṣāẽ boltī hai]{\hi{दो} \hi{भाषाएँ} \hi{बोलती} \hi{है} — counting from one word}

\label{lesson:HI-C91-sintesis-sangya}



\begin{quote}
Read this and say how many languages, before reading on.

\begin{quote}
\hi{दो} \hi{भाषाएँ} \hi{बोलती} \hi{है।}
\end{quote}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the line a paper prints}]
That clause is lifted from a personal account in the second practice paper. Until this chapter, \textbf{\hi{भाषाएँ}} was an unreadable shape.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\hi{दो} & the number \\
\hi{भाषाएँ} & the noun, carrying the plural nasal \\
\hi{बोलती} \hi{है} & the habit, and the speaker is a woman \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two things say \emph{plural} here and neither is the verb: the numeral and the ending on the noun. \textbf{The verb agrees with the person, not with the count.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
The other half of the chapter, in two lines that look almost alike:

\begin{quote}
— \hi{बच्चे} \hi{कहाँ} \hi{हैं}? — \hi{बच्चे} \hi{को} \hi{घर} \hi{भेजा।}
\end{quote}

The first \textbf{\hi{बच्चे}} is a plural and the second is one child in the oblique. \textbf{Nothing but the postposition separates them}, and a reader who misses it counts wrong.

\subsection*{How to answer}
Say each of these out loud, as a plural:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item one child, then two children
  \item one book, then two books
  \item one language, then two languages
  \item one man, then two men
\end{itemize}

The fourth is the one that sounds wrong and is right. Say it twice.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दो} \hi{भाषाएँ} \hi{बोलती} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which two words in it carry the plural
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बच्चे} \hi{को}\textquotedblright{}, and say how many children
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यह} \hi{किताब}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वह} \hi{आदमी}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the verb tell you how many? (No — it agrees with the person.) What separates a plural \textbf{\hi{बच्चे}} from an oblique one? (A postposition behind it.) Which noun shape shows no plural at all? (A masculine noun not ending in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
